fast_dct_action_tokens.What problem with per-dimension, per-tim: Think about token count (T times D per chunk) and how predictable the next token is at high control rates. Cover what that does to the per-token training signal and to dexterous, high-frequency tasks.
fast_dct_action_tokens.Why does applying a DCT along time make: Smooth signals concentrate energy in low frequencies. Explain what happens to high-frequency coefficients after scale and round, and why many zeros help the BPE stage that follows.
fast_dct_action_tokens.How do you build the orthonormal DCT-II: Give the cosine entry cos(pi(2n+1)k/2T) and the row weights sqrt(1/T) for k=0, sqrt(2/T) otherwise. Then argue the rows are orthonormal, so C times C.T is the identity.
fast_dct_action_tokens.Why flatten the coefficient matrix with: Consider what an autoregressive decoder predicts first and what it can stop early on. Cover where the informative coefficients and the long zero runs end up under each order.
fast_dct_action_tokens.Where does information get lost in the F: Name the two lossy steps: rounding and the clamp at min_token. Bound the rounding error per coefficient by 0.5/scale and use orthogonality to carry it to the actions.
fast_dct_action_tokens.How does the choice of scale trade recon: Relate scale to the rounding step size, to the range of integer values BPE must cover, and to how many high-frequency coefficients survive as non-zero.
fast_dct_action_tokens.FAST tokens with an autoregressive VLA v: Compare training speed and reuse of the language-model head against inference latency (many sequential tokens), precision limits from quantization, and decode failures on malformed token sequences.
